// question: 1
::P4Q1 One equals sign or two::[html]<p>You want the students in the 2024 batch and write\:</p><pre><code>students |&gt; filter(batch \= 2024)</code></pre><p>R refuses. What is wrong?</p>{
=[html]<p>Comparison needs <code>\=\=</code>; a single <code>\=</code> assigns rather than asks</p>#[html]<p>Correct. Use <code>filter(batch \=\= 2024)</code>.</p>
~[html]<p><code>2024</code> needs quotation marks, as <code>"2024"</code></p>#[html]<p>Not in this dataset. <code>read_csv()</code> read <code>batch</code> as a number, so <code>2024</code> is written without quotation marks. Worth checking with <code>glimpse()</code> though\: <code>&lt;dbl&gt;</code> means no quotation marks, <code>&lt;chr&gt;</code> means quotation marks.</p>
~[html]<p><code>filter()</code> works on columns, so this should be <code>select()</code></p>#[html]<p>The other way round\: <code>filter()</code> keeps <em>rows</em>, <code>select()</code> keeps <em>columns</em>. Keeping only some students is a row operation.</p>
~[html]<p>The pipe is wrong; it should be <code>students + filter(...)</code></p>#[html]<p>No. <code>|&gt;</code> is right between verbs; <code>+</code> belongs only in ggplot2, between plot layers. Primer 5 covers that distinction.</p>
####[html]<p><code>\=\=</code> asks a question; <code>\=</code> assigns a value. <code>filter()</code> needs a question, so it must be <code>filter(batch \=\= 2024)</code>. This is one of the two or three most common beginner errors in R, and dplyr's error message says so almost in those words.</p>
}

// question: 2
::P4Q2 Two conditions at once::[html]<p>What does this return?</p><pre><code>students |&gt; filter(batch \=\= 2024, attendance_pct &gt; 85)</code></pre>{
=[html]<p>Students who are in the 2024 batch <strong>and</strong> have attendance above 85</p>#[html]<p>Correct, both conditions must hold.</p>
~[html]<p>Students who are in the 2024 batch <strong>or</strong> have attendance above 85</p>#[html]<p>A comma is <em>and</em>, not <em>or</em>. For <em>or</em> you need the vertical bar\: <code>filter(batch \=\= 2024 | attendance_pct &gt; 85)</code>, which here would return far more students.</p>
~[html]<p>Two columns, <code>batch</code> and <code>attendance_pct</code></p>#[html]<p>That would be <code>select(batch, attendance_pct)</code>. <code>filter()</code> never changes which columns you have\: it only decides which rows survive, and all 17 columns come back.</p>
~[html]<p>An error, because <code>filter()</code> takes only one condition</p>#[html]<p>It takes as many as you like, separated by commas. Splitting a complicated condition across several commas is usually easier to read than joining them with <code>&amp;</code>.</p>
####[html]<p>A comma inside <code>filter()</code> means <strong>and</strong>\: a row is kept only if every condition holds. If you want <em>or</em>, you have to say so explicitly with <code>|</code>, as in <code>filter(batch \=\= 2024 | attendance_pct &gt; 85)</code>, and those two questions have very different answers, so it is worth being deliberate about which you meant.</p>
}

// question: 3
::P4Q3 One row per group::[html]<p>You want one row per <code>teaching_arm</code>, showing the number of students and their mean <code>posttest</code> score. Eleven of the 240 students have no post-test score.</p><p>Which of these gives you what you asked for?</p>{
=[html]<pre><code>students |&gt;<br>  group_by(teaching_arm) |&gt;<br>  summarise(n \= n(), mean_posttest \= mean(posttest, na.rm \= TRUE))</code></pre>#[html]<p>Correct, 76.4 in the flipped arm against 70.7 in the traditional one.</p>
~[html]<pre><code>students |&gt;<br>  group_by(teaching_arm) |&gt;<br>  summarise(n \= n(), mean_posttest \= mean(posttest))</code></pre>#[html]<p>So close. The shape is right, but <code>mean_posttest</code> comes back as <code>NA</code> for both arms\: eleven students have no post-test score, and the mean of anything containing <code>NA</code> is <code>NA</code>. Add <code>na.rm \= TRUE</code> inside <code>mean()</code>.</p>
~[html]<pre><code>students |&gt;<br>  summarise(n \= n(), mean_posttest \= mean(posttest, na.rm \= TRUE))</code></pre>#[html]<p>This gives one row for the whole cohort, not one per arm, which hides the very comparison you wanted. <code>summarise()</code> collapses everything unless <code>group_by()</code> has told it what the groups are.</p>
~[html]<pre><code>students |&gt;<br>  filter(teaching_arm) |&gt;<br>  summarise(n \= n(), mean_posttest \= mean(posttest, na.rm \= TRUE))</code></pre>#[html]<p><code>filter()</code> needs a condition, something that is <code>TRUE</code> or <code>FALSE</code>, and a column of text is neither, so this stops with an error. Splitting a table into groups is <code>group_by()</code>'s job, not <code>filter()</code>'s.</p>
####[html]<p><code>group_by()</code> then <code>summarise()</code>, with <code>na.rm \= TRUE</code> so the eleven students without a post-test do not turn both means into <code>NA</code>. Always report <code>n</code> beside a mean\: your reader needs to know whether it rests on 8 students or 80, and here the two routes to the answer (excluding inside <code>mean()</code>, or dropping those rows first) leave you with different <em>n</em>, so the number is not decoration.</p>
}

// question: 4
::P4Q4 The verbs do not edit your table::[html]<p>You run this and look at the result\:</p><pre><code>students |&gt;<br>  filter(batch \=\= 2024) |&gt;<br>  arrange(desc(attendance_pct))</code></pre><p><strong>Afterwards, the object <code>students</code> contains only the 2024 batch.</strong></p>{
~[html]<p>False</p>#[html]<p>No, the verbs never edit the table you started from. <code>students</code> still holds all 240 rows; the filtered version was printed and then discarded, because it was not assigned to anything.</p>
=[html]<p>False</p>#[html]<p>Correct. <code>students</code> is unchanged, which is also why you must assign the result if you want to keep it.</p>
####[html]<p>False. dplyr verbs return a <em>new</em> table and leave the original untouched, so you can experiment freely without damaging your data. The flip side is that a result you want to keep must be assigned to a name\: <code>students_2024 &lt;- students |&gt; filter(batch \=\= 2024)</code>. Beginners lose an afternoon to each half of this in turn.</p>
}
